Sizes & $4096^2$, $2048\times4096$, $2048\times6144$ (191 prompts each); $6144^2$ (100 prompts, \todo{E2}); $8192^2$ (12 exploratory paired prompts, metrics and qualitative examples). \\

\paragraph{Other aspect ratios.} The two non-square settings differ in which metrics favor \sca{}.  At $2048\times4096$ (factors 2 and 4) \sca{} has mixed results: ImageReward ($-0.00$ $[-0.08,0.07]$) and FID have intervals spanning zero, while the two MUSIQ scores and HPSv2 favor \sca{} and aesthetic score and CLIP-IQA favor AReA. Corrected patch FID and KID also favor AReA: patch FID is worse by 5.5 $[1.9,9.5]$ and patch KID ($\times10^3$) by 1.95 $[0.39,3.70]$. At $2048\times6144$ (factors 2 and 6) \sca{} is significantly better on ImageReward ($+0.27$ $[0.15,0.40]$), FID ($-19.8$ $[-24.4,-11.8]$), KID, Inception score, PickScore, HPSv2, both MUSIQ variants, CLIP-IQA, and ARNIQA, and significantly worse on aesthetic score ($-0.15$). Corrected patch FID and KID point estimates favor AReA at this size, but neither difference is resolved: patch FID $+3.6$ $[-0.2,11.3]$ and patch KID ($\times10^3$) $+1.70$ $[-2.22,6.07]$. The scale-2 table changes the $2048\times4096$ results negligibly (Appendix~\ref{app:ps2}). Figure~\ref{fig:gallery_8192_complete} shows four examples sampled from the completed 12-prompt exploratory $8192^2$ run; grid and stripe artifacts remain. The paired 8K scores favor \sca{} on preference and alignment, while the MUSIQ differences remain unresolved (Appendix~\ref{app:8k}). \todo{E2: $6144^2$ metrics.}

\paragraph{Latency.} \sca{}'s attention is linear in $N$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:cost}). At $4096^2$ one attention layer takes 18.7\,ms against 87.3\,ms for full attention, and a whole image 71.1\,s against 186.5\,s (Table~\ref{tab:latency}). The continuing sweep gives 18.2\,s at $2048^2$ and 40.2\,s at $3072^2$ for \sca{}, compared with 41.0 and 114.3\,s for AReA. At $6144^2$ and $8192^2$, \sca{} takes 161.6 and 287.6\,s. From $2048^2$ to $8192^2$, pixel count grows $16\times$ and measured time grows $15.8\times$. \todo{E3: finish the larger-resolution latency sweep.}

With a new table calibrated on 16 native-resolution prompts, \sca{} improves FLUX.2-dev over full attention at $4096^2$ on 50 evaluation prompts: ImageReward rises from 0.748 to 1.204, HPSv2.1 from 26.90 to 28.74, and crop MUSIQ from 38.5 to 60.0. CLIP's interval spans zero; the other nine per-image metric intervals favor \sca{}. Mean denoising-plus-decoding time falls from 444.0 to 220.2\,s, with text embeddings precomputed for both methods. This extends the full-attention comparison to a second model; it does not establish an advantage over other extrapolation methods on FLUX.2. Protocol details and all paired intervals are in Appendices~\ref{app:additional_protocols} and~\ref{app:phase2}. \todo{E9: FLUX.1-Krea-dev.}

At $2048\times4096$, \sca{} has no resolved ImageReward advantage over AReA and loses on several other metrics. Small extra figures can still appear late in sampling, the exploratory 8K gallery retains grid artifacts, and one development prompt keeps doubled limbs in every variant (Appendix~\ref{app:failures}). The opening phase was selected from development generations; the output-error objective alone did not select it. Transfer across emulated scales supports, but cannot prove, that the weights depend only on the ratio of image to window. The full 191-prompt comparison uses FLUX.1-dev and one seed per prompt; extra seeds cover 46 prompts, and the second-model comparison covers 50 prompts against full attention. UltraImage has higher preference scores under its more expensive two-stage recipe, so \sca{} does not dominate all systems or metrics. We have not run direct HRDiT or ResDiT baselines, and our guided UltraImage configuration does not cover its direct-extrapolation variant; superiority over those untested settings is unestablished. The low-sample FID estimates and automatic preference models cannot replace human evaluation, and the intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons. \todo{E2, E3, E9: the $6144^2$ comparison, remaining large-resolution latency measurements, and Krea results remain pending.}

\paragraph{End-to-end latency.} The matched $4096^2$ sweep on one GH200 gives medians of 186.5\,s for full attention (186.0, 186.6, 186.5), 202.4\,s for AReA (192.7, 202.4, 204.3), and 71.1\,s for \sca{} (71.0, 71.1, 71.1). Each method generates one excluded warm-up and then three timed images in the same process, at batch 1 and 28 steps. The earlier benchmark, retained as a separate repeat, gave (\texttt{results/latency\_4096\_batch1.csv}): full attention 184.6\,s (184.1, 184.7, 184.6), AReA 212.6\,s (207.3, 225.8, 212.6), \sca{} + band guard 88.1\,s (88.1, 98.7, 88.1; single-pass compiled band), and \sca{} final 71.0\,s (71.0, 83.1, 70.9). On the shared campaign nodes, per-image times were 71\,s for \sca{} final, 120\,s for \sca{} + band guard, and 262\,s for AReA; the campaign code used an unfused band, so dropping it saved more there (48\,s) than in the clean measurement (17\,s). At the non-square sizes we have only campaign timings on shared nodes (mean over 191 prompts): $2048\times4096$, \sca{} 38.1\,s and AReA 112.4\,s; $2048\times6144$, \sca{} 55.8\,s and AReA 150.5\,s. The two methods ran on the same pool of nodes. The continuing sweep adds clean $2048^2$ medians of 22.9\,s for full attention, 41.0\,s for AReA, and 18.2\,s for \sca{}, and $3072^2$ medians of 73.9, 114.3, and 40.2\,s, respectively; \sca{} takes 161.6\,s at $6144^2$ and 287.6\,s at $8192^2$. Each is the median of three images after a generated warm-up in the same process (\texttt{results/latency\_curve\_summary.csv}). \todo{E3: finish the larger-resolution latency sweep, Table~\ref{tab:latency}.}

We run AReA's released code with its FLUX.1 defaults (block-centre pooling, first phase for 8 of 28 steps, halo width 8, bridge ratio 0.5), the FLUX.1-dev checkpoint, guidance 4.5, 28 steps, $\mu$ at its maximum, and the seeds shared with the other methods. AReA's paper reports ImageReward 1.32 at 4K under its own settings; our shared protocol gives 0.92, so cross-paper numbers are not comparable, while our direct SCA--AReA comparison holds these settings fixed. UltraImage and FLUX.2 use the separate protocols documented above. AReA's paper reports 151\,s for AReA and 314\,s for full attention at $4096^2$ on an H100; the matched sweep measures 202.4\,s and 186.5\,s on one GH200 (medians of three images). We use commit \texttt{9e38ec2} of the released repository, which includes a cost cap on halo and bridge tokens and a jagged halo edge; neither appears in the paper text, and the paper does not say whether its Table~1 used them. Recomputed from the code with 512 text tokens, the first-phase pooling factors are 4, 4, 4, 4, 2, 2, 2, 2 at $4096\times4096$ and $2048\times4096$, and 8, 8, 8, 4, 4, 4, 2, 2 at $2048\times6144$. The second-phase windows shrink over 20 steps from 180, 151, and 192 tokens respectively to 64. At $2048\times6144$ no window is cheaper than full attention once the text tokens are counted, so the first window falls back to 192 tokens and the cap drops the bridge and halo on the first three second-phase steps. Other differences from the release defaults are the FLUX.1-dev checkpoint instead of FLUX.1-Krea-dev, and one seed per prompt shared across methods instead of one seed for all prompts. \todo{E9: AReA with its default FLUX.1-Krea-dev checkpoint, against recalibrated \sca{}.}
